1:
The chapter opens with the barest of narrative hinges — Elihu resumes, having paused to see whether any voice would answer him — and the witnesses use the lull to set the whole speech in view. The reformed John Gill pictures the interval: Elihu, having spoken, waited awhile to observe whether any of the company would rise to contradict and refute him, or declare their assent; or rather to see whether Job himself would make reply. Perceiving no inclination in Job to answer, he proceeded to take notice of certain other undue expressions the sufferer had let fall, and to refute them. The single word "moreover," Gill implies, marks a fresh charge laid on top of the last, the debate resumed not because Job had spoken but because he had fallen silent.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the argument of the speech in a sentence, as a table of contents for what follows: Elihu accuses Job of impious speeches; he will show that no man can affect God by his iniquity nor profit him by his righteousness; and that many are afflicted and oppressed, yet few cry to God for help, and for want of faith continue in their affliction. The three movements Clarke names — the charge, the greatness of God, and the unanswered cry — are the skeleton on which the rest of the chapter hangs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns at once to Elihu's method, which is to appeal not over Job's head but to Job's own conscience. Before he states the bad words he means to reprove, Elihu asks, in effect, "Thinkest thou this to be right?" — referring the very judgment of the matter to the man he reproves, and recurring, as Henry notes, to his old maxim that God is greater than man (ch. 33:12). Henry reads in this a confidence that truth and equity, sooner or later, will have every man's conscience on their side, and a good opinion of Job besides: Elihu thought better of him than his hasty words suggested, and believed that, once the mistake was shown him, Job would not stand to it. When we have said in haste what was not right, Henry adds, it becomes us to own that our second thoughts convict us it was wrong. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the speech begins in courtesy — a pause, an appeal to conscience, a charge framed as a question — and that Elihu comes forward not as an accuser hunting a hypocrite but as one who would recall a good man from a rash word he had let slip about the justice of God.
2:
"Thinkest thou this to be right," Elihu begins, "that thou saidst, My righteousness is more than God's?" — and the witnesses divide at once over whether the sufferer ever said such a thing. The reformed John Gill takes the appeal as directed straight to Job's own conscience and reason: as a natural man guided by the light of nature, and still more as a good man who feared God and knew so much of him, Job could never, on sober reflection, think it right — what he had said concerning God and his justice. Gill lets the charge stand as a fair inference from Job's speeches, a word that Job's better self would disown once it was held up to him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the grammar of the ponderous sentence, taking the neutral "this" to point forward to what follows in v.3: dost thou consider this right, and think on that account to set thy righteousness above the divine — as though no righteousness on God's side answered to thine, because he makes no distinction between a man's righteousness and his sin, and lets the former go unrewarded? They render the disputed clause flatly, "my righteousness exceedeth God's," the preposition comparative as at ch. 32:2.

Against this the wesleyan-arminian voices protest that Job said no such thing. Adam Clarke calls the words as they stand a blasphemous saying that Job never uttered, directly or by construction, and would render the Hebrew rather "I am righteous before God": whatever Job was in his friends' eyes, he knew that in God's sight he was a righteous man — and he had a right to the character, Clarke insists, because God himself had given it to him. John Wesley agrees that Job never said this in express terms, but only things from which it might seem to follow, namely that God had punished him more than he deserved.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds the two sides together. Job had not said it in so many words, yet what he had said was capable of being so represented and perhaps seemed to involve it (compare ch. 9:22 and ch. 10:15); here again, Ellicott judges, was a misrepresentation of Job's meaning. For Job never meant that he was none the better for being righteous — that he had expressly denied — but it was perfectly true that he had said his righteousness had not delivered him from suffering. So the debate is real and turns on a single preposition: whether Elihu reports Job's mind or a caricature of it, and whether the Hebrew says "more than God" or only "righteous before God."
3:
The second half of the alleged saying draws the same treatment — a charge inferred, not quoted — as Elihu presses the complaint that religion had brought Job no return. The reformed John Gill grants that Job had said, in effect, that his righteousness was of no avail to him, that he received no more benefit by being righteous than by being wicked, since God destroys the one as well as the other and his integrity had not fenced him from calamity. Yet Gill is careful that this too is an inference from Job's words rather than his express assertion. And he turns the complaint into a distinction: a man's own righteousness is indeed of no advantage as to justification before God or the title to salvation, but it is of great advantage otherwise — a defence against the calumnies of wicked men, a thing honourable among men, and the ground of that rejoicing which is the testimony of a good conscience.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the words as spoken, half-bitterly, toward God himself: "My righteousness cannot profit thee, nor do I find that it is of any benefit to myself." Or else, he allows, Elihu is stating in general the charge he will afterwards make good — that Job had reasoned how his religion might profit him, and had asked what he should gain by righteousness more than by sin. John Wesley smooths the grammar, noting that the "unto thee" is really "unto me," such changes of person being frequent in Hebrew, so that the sense is, "God does not reward me so much as I deserve." But Wesley joins Gill and Clarke in the caution that governs the whole exchange: it was not fair to charge this upon Job, which he had neither directly nor indirectly affirmed.

The complaint Elihu fastens on, the witnesses agree, is the oldest and most dangerous in the book — the suspicion, voiced by the psalmist when he compared his own troubles with the ease of the wicked, that a man has cleansed his heart in vain (Ps. 73:13). It is the very question the prospering sinners of an earlier chapter had flung at heaven, "What profit shall we have if we pray unto him?" — words Job had himself repudiated, putting the counsel of the wicked far from him (ch. 21:15-16). Whether Elihu is just in laying them again at Job's door is the point on which the witnesses press their protest; but none of them doubts that the sentiment, if it were Job's, would be a wronging of the God who gives his servants better than they deserve. To disown the profit of religion because affliction had come, they hold, is to make God a debtor to man, and that is precisely the error the rest of the speech is bent on curing.
4:
Before he opens his reply Elihu widens its address, undertaking to answer not Job only but "thy companions with thee," and the witnesses ask who these companions are. The reformed John Gill rules out the three friends whom the Septuagint here names, since they were not on Job's side but rather, like Eliphaz, on Elihu's own; the companions must be all who think as Job thinks, whether present or absent, in whatsoever part of the world — for the answer Elihu is about to give would serve to confute the bad notion of God in whomsoever it were found. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the promise as a pledge to make good what the friends had left undone: "I will show thee the evil of a sinful way, and the benefit of righteousness, and supply what thy friends have omitted in their discourses with thee."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, weighs the promise against the performance and finds Elihu less original than he claims. Elihu professes to answer Job's friends as well as Job, yet what he actually says in the verses following is very much what Eliphaz had urged before — that God is too high to be affected by man's righteousness or unrighteousness (ch. 22:3) — and what Bildad had said in his brief last speech (ch. 25). Ellicott concedes the premise: it is indeed true that God is too exalted to be touched by human conduct. But he presses the flaw in the inference. It does not follow that God is therefore indifferent to that conduct; for were he indifferent he would not be a righteous judge, and a righteous judge is exactly what the argument means to vindicate.

So the verse, brief as it is, sets the terms of the whole reply and its weakness at once. Elihu speaks as one confident that a single answer will silence a whole party of the like-minded, and the witnesses let that confidence stand. But Ellicott's caution hangs over it: the great truth Elihu is about to build on — the sheer height of God above the reach of man — is true, and yet a half-truth, capable of proving too much. If God gains nothing by our righteousness and loses nothing by our sin, it may seem to follow that our conduct is nothing to him; and that conclusion, drawn too fast, would unsay the very justice Elihu has risen to defend. The witnesses do not divide over the doctrine; they only mark, with Ellicott, that a true premise in an over-eager mouth can be pushed to a false end, and that Elihu will have to be read with that danger in view.
5:
Elihu grounds his whole argument in a gesture upward — "Look unto the heavens, and see; and behold the clouds" — and the witnesses read the summons as an ocular demonstration of the distance between God and man. The reformed John Gill keeps the sense plain and physical: the firmament of heaven, with its sun and moon and stars, and above it the clouds, all set visibly beyond the reach of the man who is bidden to gaze up at them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the second word. The clouds are the shechakim, which the Vulgate renders the "ethers," from a root meaning to contend or fight together — the agitated and conflicting air and light whose strong commotion produces both light and heat; the bare sight of these, Clarke says, is enough to show a man that God is infinitely beyond him in wisdom and excellence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the argument out of the picture. The heavens and clouds are far above us, and God is infinitely above them; how much, then, is he set out of the reach either of our sins or of our services. God made man erect and bade him look up to heaven; the idolaters looked up and worshipped the host of heaven, the sun and moon and stars, but we are to look up and worship the Lord of that host. Higher than the visible heavens is his glory, Henry adds, echoing the psalm that sets God's glory above the heavens (Ps. 8:1), and higher than heaven is the knowledge of him (ch. 11:8). The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley compresses the inference to its point: the clouds are far above us, and God far above them, so how much is he out of the reach either of our sins or our services.

The witnesses do not divide; together they turn a simple upward glance into the premise of the argument. The height that a man cannot climb is made the emblem of a majesty a man cannot touch. Whatever we do beneath the clouds — the best of our righteousness, the worst of our sin — rises no nearer to the throne above them than the dust of the field rises to the stars. Yet the very figure carries, unspoken, the danger that had been flagged at v.4: a God so high might seem a God too high to care. The witnesses let the image do its proper work here, humbling the man who would make God his debtor, and leave to the following verses the task of drawing out exactly what does, and does not, follow from the immeasurable distance between the clouds and the One who rides above them.
6:
"If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him?" — the question is a challenge flung at the sinner, and the witnesses hear in it the impotence of all human malice against God. The reformed John Gill grants everything to the reality of sin and then denies it any power to wound: sin is against God, contrary to his nature, a breach of his law, a contempt of his authority, a thing he hates and abhors; and yet he cannot be so touched by it as to be ruffled or discomposed, his peace disturbed or his happiness broken in upon, for the affections ascribed to him are spoken only after the manner of men. Still less can he be hurt or endangered or dethroned. Men can no more reach him by a hostile act than they can arrest the sun in its course or pluck it from its orbit. Or, Gill adds from Broughton's rendering, "what canst thou work for him?" — no atonement, no satisfaction for sin, is in a sinner's power to make.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same defiance further. It speaks much for the greatness and glory of God, he says, that it is not in the power of his worst enemies to do him any real prejudice. Sin is called a thing "against God" because the sinner so intends it and God so takes it, an injury aimed at his honour; and yet it can do nothing against him. The malice of sinners is an impotent malice: it cannot destroy his being or his perfections, cannot dethrone him from his power and dominion, cannot disturb his peace, defeat his counsels, nor derogate from his essential glory. It follows, Henry concludes, that Job spoke amiss if he asked what he was profited by being cleansed from his sin, for God was no gainer by his reformation — and if not God, then who but Job himself.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the whole in a line: God is neither benefited by a man's righteousness nor injured by his iniquity, however multiplied it may be. And the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the run of verses together, set the couplet in its logic — if thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? — the heaping of the offences only sharpening the point that their sum still touches nothing above the clouds. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the verse strips a sinner of the last flattering thought that his rebellion matters to God as an injury, and so prepares the counter-truth of the verse to come (v.7), that if his sin cannot harm God, neither can his goodness enrich him, and the whole account of profit and loss must be struck between man and man, not between man and heaven.
7:
Having shown that sin cannot injure God, Elihu turns the coin over — "if thou be righteous, what givest thou him?" — and the witnesses answer that a man's goodness adds as little to God as his evil takes away. The reformed John Gill roots the point in the source of all righteousness. Whatever righteousness any creature has is God's before it is the creature's: the holiness of the angels in heaven, the innocence of Adam in his first estate, the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers and the grace of holiness implanted in them, and even the works of righteousness they do — all are wrought under his influence, by his grace and in his strength. A man can therefore give God nothing of his own, and God, being all-sufficient, needs nothing; even the goodness of the saints, the psalmist owns, extends not to God but to one another (Ps. 16:2-3), and much less any goodness of ours. Our best works of righteousness are a debt we owe him, not a gift we bestow; and though they may add to his manifestative glory, both in those who do them and in those who see them, they can add nothing at all to his essential glory.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reaches the same conclusion by the shorter road of God's self-sufficiency. If a man be righteous, what does he give to God? He needs not our service; or if the work were to be done, he has better hands than ours at his command. Our religion brings no accession whatever to his felicity. So far is he from being beholden to us, Henry says, that we are wholly beholden to him — for making us righteous in the first place and for accepting the righteousness he has made. From which it follows that we can demand nothing from him as of right, and have no reason to complain when we do not receive what we expect, but every reason to be thankful that we receive far better than we deserve.

The two witnesses do not divide, and their agreement quietly dismantles the grievance Elihu is answering. Job had seemed to reckon his piety a kind of investment on which heaven owed him a return; the challenge "what receiveth he of thine hand?" cancels the debt before it can be claimed. There is a strange comfort folded into the humbling, for if God gains nothing by our obedience he cannot be tempted, as men are, to prefer the useful servant to the faithful one, nor to withhold his mercy until we have paid him back. The witnesses leave the verse where Elihu meant it to rest: God is no man's debtor, and the creature who would put him in his debt has mistaken both the giver and the gift. What remains — and the next verse will say it (v.8) — is that our conduct, powerless to reach God, is far from powerless toward our fellow men.
8:
If neither sin nor righteousness reaches God, the verse names where they do reach — "a man as thou art," "the son of man" — and the witnesses read it as the necessary complement to all that has gone before. The reformed John Gill unfolds the harm first. A man's wickedness may wound himself, his body through debauchery and intemperance, his family and estate by wasting them, and above all his soul, for every sin is an injury to the sinner's soul and exposes it to ruin; it harms even a good man, breaking in upon his peace and hindering his communion with God; and it harms his neighbours, frail and mortal like himself, whether by the ill example that leads them astray or by the murder, adultery, and theft that fall directly upon their persons and estates. Because sin is thus hurtful to others, Gill notes, God resents it and punishes it, even though, strictly speaking, it cannot hurt him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers to render the verse flatly and let its balance speak: "to a man like thyself is thy wickedness, and to the son of man thy righteousness." Thou mayest injure thyself and others by thy wickedness, he paraphrases, and thou mayest benefit both by thy righteousness — but God thou canst neither hurt nor profit. The whole moral weight of a man's life, on Clarke's reading, is discharged sideways, upon his fellows, and never upward.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry completes the thought on its brighter side. Men may indeed be either bettered or damaged by what we do; a wicked man may wound or rob or slander his neighbour, or draw him into sin and so prejudice his very soul, while a man's justice, charity, wisdom, and piety may profit the son of man — for our goodness, as the psalmist says, extends to the saints that are in the earth (Ps. 16:3). And in both these, Henry insists, the sovereign Judge of all interests himself: he will reward those who do good and punish those who do hurt to their fellow-creatures and fellow-subjects. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Elihu is not teaching a cold indifference in God — as if, our conduct being nothing to him, he cared nothing how we used it — but drawing the line exactly: God is beyond our reach, our neighbour is not, and it is on the ground of what we do to our neighbour that the God who cannot be touched himself will nevertheless call us to account. The distance that humbled the sinner in the earlier verses becomes here the very thing that secures his responsibility, for the Judge who gains nothing is for that reason perfectly impartial in the reckoning he keeps between man and man.
9:
The argument turns from the individual to the crowd of the wronged — "by reason of the multitude of oppressions they make the oppressed to cry" — and the witnesses see Elihu taking up a fresh complaint of Job's, that heaven seems deaf to the outcry of the afflicted. The reformed John Gill reads the verse as either an instance of the harm just spoken of or a new charge to be met: the poor are oppressed by the rich, whose wealth gives them a power they abuse, and the weak by the mighty, until, like Israel under the taskmasters, they are made to cry out by reason of their oppressors. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the complaint outright and traces it to Job's own earlier words, that men groan from out of the city and the soul of the wounded cries out, yet God lays not folly to the oppressors (ch. 24:12). Is there a righteous God, Job had seemed to ask, and can it be that he should so slowly hear, so slowly see?

Henry gives Elihu's solution, which the other witnesses share: if the cry is not heard, the fault lies not in God, who is ever ready to hear and help, but in the criers themselves, who ask and have not because they ask amiss (James 4:3). Theirs is a complaining, wailing cry wrung out by the arm of the mighty, not a penitent praying cry; the cry of nature and passion, not of grace — like those who, the prophet says, howled upon their beds but cried not unto God with their heart (Hos. 7:14). The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the crowd the same way: the wicked rich oppress the wicked poor, who shout aloud because of their oppressors yet find no relief, because they call not upon God.

The grammatical-historical witnesses set the verse in the argument's frame. Charles Ellicott states its logic: among men there may indeed be oppression, but not with an almighty and righteous Judge, so that the right course under a tyrant's arm is to wait — men may well complain of an earthly oppressor, "but how canst thou say thou beholdest Him not?" Keil and Delitzsch, gathering the run of verses, note that the address is not aimed at Job alone but treats first of the acts of injustice that prevail among men and seem to go unpunished, and then turns upon Job, who had complained in just this way that his own prayer went unanswered (ch. 30:20). The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the sob of the oppressed is real, and that its going unanswered is no reproach to God's justice but a symptom of the sufferer's own heart, which cries against the oppressor without once crying to the Maker who alone could lift the arm that crushes it.
10:
"But none saith, Where is God my maker, who giveth songs in the night" — and the witnesses find in the unspoken question the reason the outcry goes unheard. The reformed John Gill reads the plural "my makers" of the one God — Father, Son, and Spirit — who made all men, and laments that not one of the oppressed, or scarcely one, so much as inquires after him, seeks him for deliverance, or desires his gracious presence in their distress; they do not consider him the author of their being, nor its preserver, nor their kind benefactor, and that is why they are not heard. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that they have no just apprehension of God's being, and dwells on the beautiful clause that follows, "who giveth songs in the night." He gathers its renderings — the Chaldee's "before whom the high angels give praise in the night," the Septuagint's "who sets the night-watches," the Syriac and Arabic "gives meditations in the night," Coverdale's "that shineth upon us that we might praise him in the night" — and draws the comfort that a holy soul has continual communion with God, whose praise is the subject of its songs by night and day. John Wesley reads the Maker as the one "who alone made me, and who only can deliver me," and who, when our condition is darkest, can turn our darkness into light and put a new song in our mouth.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, unsettles the familiar reading. Some render the line, he notes, so that it is the oppressor who is meant — "but he who giveth songs in the night saith not, Where is God my Maker?" — the selfish and luxurious man who spends the night in feasting and revelry; an intelligible sense. And the proverbial beauty of "songs in the night" notwithstanding, Ellicott doubts whether, taken of God, it is so obvious here, since it would ascribe to him the turning of the night of affliction into joy, an office often assigned to God but of no very manifest fitness in this place. The decision, he says, partly turns on whether the words "Where is God my Maker?" are the cry the oppressed fail to utter, or the words of Elihu himself — and Ellicott leans to the latter as the more intelligible.

So the verse carries a genuine disagreement over who sings and who asks. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, standing with the majority, presses the devotional point regardless of the grammar: afflictions are sent to quicken us to inquire early after God (compare Eccl. 12:1), yet of the many who groan under oppression, few ever say, "Where is God my Maker?" — few repent, few return to him that smites them, few seek that comfort in his favour which would outweigh the trouble. It is lamentable, Henry adds, that all are asking where is mirth, where is wealth, where is a good bargain, and none is asking after the God who gave them breath. The witnesses do not finally divide over the lesson, only over the construction: whether the songs in the night are God's gift to the afflicted or the reveller's ease, and whether the great missing question is the sufferer's or the preacher's own.
11:
The unasked question of the last verse carries a clause that measures how far the ungrateful have fallen — God "teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wiser than the fowls of heaven" — and the witnesses turn it into a rebuke. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the beasts are taught and know much, some of them a great deal, but not so much as man, whom God has raised far above them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the contrast to a sting, borrowing the prophet's complaint that the ox knows his owner and the ass his master's crib, but Israel does not know, my people do not consider (Isa. 1:3). Beasts and birds, and even the fish of the pond, know and seem thankful to the hand that feeds them, while man, made nobler than they and gifted with the highest powers, considers not the Lord nor discerns the operation of his hand; the brute creatures, Clarke says bitterly, have more gratitude to their masters than man has to his God. John Wesley reads the clause as the very aggravation of that neglect: God has given men what he denied the beasts, wisdom to know God and themselves, and so leaves them without excuse when they will not use that wisdom to call upon him in the time of trouble.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the thought into its proper use. This nobler endowment furnishes matter for thanksgiving even under the heaviest affliction, for whatever else is stripped away, the immortal soul is left, a jewel of more worth than all the world; and it is a reason we should, under our troubles, inquire after God our Maker. The chief excellency of reason, Henry says, is that it makes us capable of religion, and it is in this above all that we are taught more than the beasts and the fowls: they have wonderful instincts for finding their food and their shelter, but none of them can ask, "Where is God my Maker?" God relieves the brute creatures when they cry to him according to the best of their capacity (Ps. 104:21); but if the oppressed only cry out under the arm of the mighty and never look up, they do no more than the brutes, who also complain when they are hurt, and they forget the wisdom that was meant to lift them so far above them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a quieter alternative to the whole clause, that it may be read "who teacheth us by the beasts of the earth, and maketh us wise by the fowls of heaven" — the creatures themselves becoming our instructors, so that the oppression is the more culpable for making its victims forget that the God who has favoured man above the beasts, and without whom not one sparrow falls, has surely not forgotten the men who are of more value than many sparrows. The witnesses do not divide on the reproach they draw. Whether man is taught more than the beasts or taught by them, the shame is the same: that the one creature able to seek his Maker in the dark should cry, when he is hurt, no better than the ox that lows in the yard.
12:
The cry rises again in this verse and again meets silence — "there they cry, but none giveth answer" — and the witnesses part over the cause the verse assigns, "the pride of evil men." The reformed John Gill hears the oppressed crying as the brutes cry, by reason of their sufferings, but without any due sense of God's hand upon them or of his being their only helper and deliverer, and so their cry falls to the ground. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the closing phrase of the oppressors: the word, he says, means "from the face, presence, or influence of the pride of wicked men," so that the afflicted cry for deliverance from the pride of their oppressors — yet they are not heard, and the reason is the one Elihu keeps returning to, that they cry not to God at all. On Clarke's reading the pride named is the tyrant's, the thing cried against, and the unanswered prayer fails for a separate reason, its misdirection.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley read the pride the other way, as the criers' own. Henry sees them lying and exclaiming against their oppressors, filling every ear with complaint and not sparing to reflect on God himself, yet none gives answer — and none, because of the pride of evil men, for they are evil men who regard iniquity in their hearts, and God will not hear such (Ps. 66:18); he hears only the desire of the humble (Ps. 10:17) and delivers those whom he has first, by his grace, prepared and made fit for deliverance. Affliction is sent to hide pride from a man; if under it the heart stays unhumbled and the pride unmortified, the sufferer has himself to thank that the trouble is not removed. Wesley states it flatly: God does not answer their cries because they are at once evil — wicked and impenitent — and proud, unhumbled for the very sins that brought the misery upon them.

So the witnesses divide, not over the doctrine but over the grammar of a single clause: whether "the pride of evil men" names the oppressors whose arrogance wrings out the cry, or the oppressed whose unbroken pride stops the cry at heaven's door. Clarke keeps the two thoughts apart, the pride the tyrant's and the failure the sufferer's misdirected prayer; Henry and Wesley fold them into one, making the criers' own pride the reason for the silence. The witnesses do not divide, however, on the moral Elihu is pressing: that a cry which is all complaint and no penitence, whether choked by the oppressor's arrogance or by the sufferer's own, is not the cry that moves the God who stoops only to the humble.
13:
Elihu now states the principle beneath the silence — "surely God will not hear vanity, neither will the Almighty regard it" — and the witnesses weigh what the "vanity" is that God refuses to hear. The reformed John Gill ranges over the word's force. It may be rendered "a lie," than which nothing is more abominable to God, who is nigh only to those that call upon him in truth; or "that which is rash," the prayer flung up in passion and a revengeful spirit, as the cry of the oppressed so often is; or plainly vain and empty prayers — vain in their matter, being only for outward mercies and worldly goods and not for the things that are according to the will of God, asked that they may be consumed upon the lusts of the flesh (James 4:3), and vain in their manner, being offered neither in the name of Christ nor under the influence of his Spirit, nor with reverence, nor with sincerity of soul. Such prayer God will not hear, for he searches the heart and requires truth in the inward part.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reduces the verse to its plainest edge: God will not attend to such vain cries; the oppressed cry from their oppressions, but they cry not to God, and a cry that never reaches him he cannot be said to hear. On this reading the verse simply seals the diagnosis of the preceding lines — the outcry fails not because heaven is deaf but because the prayer is hollow.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers a different way of construing the sentence altogether. Some, he observes, take it not as Elihu's own verdict but as a continuation of the oppressed men's cry from the verse before, their own despairing conclusion: "seeing it is all in vain, God doth not hear, neither doth the Almighty regard it." On that construction the words are the very murmur of unbelief that Elihu is exposing, the sufferers charging God with the deafness that is in truth their own. The witnesses do not finally divide over the drift of the passage. Whether the sentence is Elihu's principle — that a vain and hypocritical prayer is no prayer God will heed — or the oppressed's complaint that their prayer goes for nothing, both readings serve the one argument he is building: that the unanswered cry convicts the crier, not the God he cries to, and that the remedy is not a louder complaint but a truer one, offered in humility and faith to the Maker the sufferer has all this while neglected to seek.
14:
"Although thou sayest thou shalt not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust thou in him" — with this the address turns from the crowd of the oppressed directly back to Job, and the witnesses read it as Elihu's answer to a despairing word. The reformed John Gill is careful to say what the "seeing" is not. God is invisible in his essence, yet is seen in his works of creation and providence, which Job knew; he is seen in Christ by the eye of faith, in whom Job had trusted as his salvation; and he will be seen in the beatific vision hereafter, of which Job was fully persuaded. The "not seeing," then, is none of these, but Job's despair of ever seeing God upon a throne of judgment, hearing his cause and acquitting him — a sight he had often longed for and given up as hopeless.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the complaint two ways, both improper: that Job could not understand the meaning of God's severe dealings with him (ch. 23:8-9), and that he despaired of ever seeing God's gracious returns, giving all up for lost like Hezekiah when he said, "I shall not see the Lord" (Isa. 38:11). In prosperity, Henry observes, we think our mountain will never be brought low, and in adversity that our valley will never be filled — both as absurd as to think fair or foul weather must last for ever. But when Job looked up to God, Henry says, he had no reason to speak so despairingly, for "judgment is before him": God has the whole plan of his providence before him and does all in wisdom and justice, and there is a day of judgment coming when the seeming disorders will be set right and the dark chapters expounded; then shall Job see his face with joy. Therefore, Henry urges with the verse, trust in him, depend upon him, and wait, believing the issue will be good at last (Isa. 30:18).

The wesleyan-arminian voices second the counsel. Adam Clarke notes that several manuscripts and the Septuagint read "thou shalt not see me" or "us," the unpointed Hebrew allowing either, but keeps the sense fixed: God has forgotten neither to punish nor to save, so trust him, and choose to be a monument of his mercy rather than of his justice. John Wesley paraphrases the whole as a promise that though God may for a season delay to answer, he will certainly do right, justice being ever before his tribunal; and so, instead of murmuring, Job is to repent of the past, humble himself under God's hand, and wait patiently in his way till deliverance come — for come it will, if he does not himself hinder it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only the sharper rendering of the first clause, "thou dost not behold him," turning Job's flat denial into a present blindness that the counsel to trust is meant to cure. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's "I shall not see him" is a word of unbelief, and that the medicine for it is not a clearer sight but a firmer trust in the God whose judgment, though unseen, is sure.
15:
The book itself calls no verse harder than this, and the witnesses frankly own its obscurity even as they divide over its sense — "but now, because it is not so, he hath visited in his anger; yet he knoweth it not in great extremity." The reformed John Gill keeps the first clause of Job: "because it is not so" means because there was not in Job that trust, hope, patience, and quiet expectation that God would appear for him and do him open justice; for though he had confidence of an interest in his living Redeemer and of eternal life, he had not, as he ought, the assurance that God would bring his cause to the light and let him behold his righteousness. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet to the same effect and carry it into the next verse — because it is not so, God has visited in his anger, and Job, in his great extremity, does not know it — so that the visitation of wrath is real and Job's ignorance of its meaning is precisely his fault. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way and names the wound in it: because Job did not thus trust, the affliction that came at first from love now has displeasure mixed with it, God visiting him in anger and taking it ill that he cannot find in his heart to trust him; where there are mixtures of divine wrath in our troubles, Henry says, we may thank ourselves, for it is because we quarrel with God and distrust his providence (Prov. 19:3).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reverses the polarity of the verse. He renders it rather "because he visiteth not in his anger," which he calls the more literal reading, and finds the sense to be that because vengeance is not speedily executed upon an evil work, the hearts of men are emboldened to do iniquity — and this, he says, is in effect the very charge Elihu brings against Job. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses the clause "very obscure," surveys the rival constructions, and comes down near Clarke. The Authorised Version, he notes, refers the first clause to God and the second to Job; but he would rather render that what God's anger has visited upon Job is as nothing compared with his deserts, and that God has not regarded the great abundance of his sin — that is, has not visited it with anger. The word behind "arrogance" or "abundance," Ellicott adds, occurs nowhere else and seems to mean superfluity; and whatever rendering is chosen, the general bearing is that Job is encouraged in his murmuring because God has dealt with him too leniently — though happily, he remarks, the judgment was not to be long deferred (ch. 38:1).

So the witnesses genuinely disagree over the verse's very drift. Gill, Henry, and Keil and Delitzsch keep the received reading, in which God has visited Job in anger because Job would not trust him; Clarke and Ellicott turn it about, so that God has not yet visited in anger, and it is that forbearance which has emboldened the sufferer's complaint. The one reading makes the verse a rebuke for distrust punished, the other a rebuke for leniency abused; yet under either the moral is one, and the witnesses close upon it together — that Job has mistaken the silence of God, reading as absence or injustice what is in truth either a chastening he will not understand or a patience he has presumed upon.
16:
The speech ends on its verdict, and the witnesses take Elihu's closing sentence — that Job "doth open his mouth in vain" and "multiplieth words without knowledge" — as his summing-up of the whole. The reformed John Gill refers it to the unbecoming expressions Job had let fall in his loud complaints of God and in the defence of himself: all that speech was to no purpose, because it did not spring from the trust and humility that alone could have profited him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same futility across all that Job had said. Job opens his mouth in vain, whether in complaining of his grievances and crying for redress or in justifying himself and clearing his own innocency, because he does not trust in God and wait for him nor pay a due regard to him in his afflictions; he had said a great deal, multiplied words, but all without knowledge, because he did not encourage himself in God nor humble himself before him — and the man who distrusts God, Henry warns, must not think that he shall receive anything from him (James 1:7). Yet Henry is careful to mark how gently Elihu handles him. Unlike the three friends, he does not condemn Job for a hypocrite, but charges him only with Moses's fault — speaking unadvisedly with his lips when his spirit was provoked; and when we are told of such a fault, Henry adds, it is a mercy, to be taken as patiently and kindly as Job took it, not repeating but recanting what we have said amiss.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes first the doctrine of the delay: God will execute vengeance when it may best serve the ends of his justice, providence, and mercy, and the deferring of judgment is no proof it will not fall, any more than the deferring of mercy proves that God has forgotten to be gracious. But on the last clause Clarke turns the reproof about with disarming candour. "He multiplieth words without knowledge" — however this may apply to Job, it applies, he says, very strongly and generally not only to the words of Job's three friends but to those of Elihu himself; for the whole contest has frequently been a mere strife of words. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the verse as the close of the run, let it stand plainly as the charge it is: Job has opened his mouth in vain and heaped up words without knowledge.

The witnesses do not divide over the verdict, and Clarke's aside only deepens it. Elihu drops the curtain on his third speech convinced that Job's torrent of self-defence has been so much wasted breath, spoken without the one thing that would have given it weight, a humble trust in the God he was arraigning. That the same censure, as Clarke owns, might be turned back upon the speakers who pronounce it — the friends and Elihu alike — does not blunt its truth for Job; it only reminds the reader that in this long war of words the sufferer was not the only one who talked past his knowledge, and that the God who will soon answer out of the whirlwind will have something to say to more mouths than one.
